stances.claim: With due respect, the Philippine government may have lost credibility under the Rome Statute's 'unwilling or unable genuinely' test because PBBM publicly defended Duterte and Dela Rosa without first conducting a trustworthy, transparent, and thorough investigation -- amounting to presidential prejudgment.
stances.rhetorical_move: Diplomatic-respectful framing of a hard credibility critique.

stances.claim: Congressional resolutions defending the former president and Sen. Dela Rosa, plus the presidential prejudgment, may have tainted DOJ and OSG officials with bias despite their personal talent and respectability.
stances.rhetorical_move: Separates institutional taint from individual capacity -- preserves respect while diagnosing the strategic problem.

stances.claim: The best way to stop the ICC is to create -- via executive order -- a credible, competent, and independent body modeled on the 1983 Agrava Board, to investigate and prosecute the drug-war killings, identify the masterminds, and observe both speed and due process.
stances.rhetorical_move: Constructive-proposal closure pivoting from diagnosis to prescription, with named historical template.

stances.claim: Without such a credible local mechanism, the ICC will likely proceed -- and the Philippines will be 'mercilessly debased and numbered among failed African states which have been ICC's prowling grounds.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Reputational consequence framing reinforcing the urgency of the proposal.

stances.claim: Even if Duterte and Dela Rosa themselves agreed in interviews to face investigation by Filipinos but not by ICC foreign judges, the defense mounted by PBBM and the legislators 'minimized the duo's posture and maximized the possibility of the ICC's assertion' of jurisdiction.
stances.rhetorical_move: Nuanced disaggregation: distinguishes the accuseds' posture from the government's defense.

notable_anecdotes.description: The ICC institutional structure laid out: 18 judges total elected by member-states for staggered nine-year terms; Pre-Trial Chamber composed of 3 judges; Appeals Chamber composed of 5 judges (the Court president plus 4 others, different from the PTC). The OSG's appeal brief was due March 13, 2023, with the AC's decision expected in about four months (August) per normal timeline, possibly with oral arguments.
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Procedural-architecture exposition for readers unfamiliar with ICC structure.

notable_anecdotes.description: Disparity in drug-war death counts: 6,252 per the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) figure reported in the Feb. 28 Inquirer editorial vs. 30,000 estimated by critics.
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Frames the scale dispute at the heart of the ICC inquiry.

notable_anecdotes.description: Modern remote-evidence capacity: 'If the AC rules against the OSG, the ICC prosecutor need not come physically to our country because the testimonies of witnesses, including the relatives of the victims, could be taken abroad, and the documentary evidence brought and authenticated abroad also. With the use of advanced technology, physical presence can be dispensed with.'
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Removes a possible reassurance -- sovereign refusal of physical entry will not block the prosecution.

notable_anecdotes.description: The Agrava Board template: 'When faced with the humongous public outcry for justice due to the assassination of Ninoy Aquino in 1983 -- with many fingers pointing at him and his trusted officials as the culprits -- the late strongman created an impartial body, the Agrava Board composed of credible and independent members to identify and prosecute the true killers.'
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Marcos-Sr.-era precedent invoked as the strategic template for Marcos-Jr.-era action -- a pointed historical parallel.

one_paragraph_summary: Following reader questions on his Feb. 27 column (A116), CJ Panganiban offers the title-thesis answer: the best way to stop the ICC from investigating and prosecuting alleged drug-war crimes -- a scenario the Inquirer's Feb. 28 editorial called 'a nightmare' -- is for the administration to create an independent and credible panel modeled on Ferdinand Marcos Sr.'s 1983 Agrava Board (formed to investigate Ninoy Aquino's assassination). He first lays out the procedural state of play: the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber has granted Prosecutor Karim Khan authority to investigate drug-war killings estimated by PDEA at 6,252 and by critics at 30,000; the OSG had secured a suspension; Khan announced resumption, dissatisfied with slow DOJ action; the OSG appealed to the ICC Appeals Chamber (5 judges including the Court president, different from the PTC, among the 18 total ICC judges serving nine-year staggered terms). The OSG brief was due March 13, with an AC decision expected by August. CJ warns that even an adverse ruling would not require physical entry -- modern technology allows witness testimony and document authentication abroad. Under the Rome Statute's complementarity principle, the ICC defers only if the state is 'investigating or prosecuting' and is not 'unwilling or unable genuinely' -- where 'genuinely' means 'trustworthy, transparent, and thorough.' With due respect, CJ argues, the government has likely lost credibility under this test because PBBM publicly defended Duterte and Sen. Dela Rosa as alleged main perpetrators without first conducting any trustworthy/transparent/thorough investigation -- amounting to presidential prejudgment that, with congressional resolutions defending the former president, taints DOJ and OSG officials despite their personal talent and respectability. Duterte and Dela Rosa, for their part, have said they would face investigation and prosecution 'by Filipinos' but not by ICC foreign judges. The administration's strategic dilemma resolves in the Agrava Board template: a credible, competent, independent body created by executive order to investigate drug-war killings, identify masterminds, and judge with both speed and due process -- sparing 'our one and only Motherland... shame and ignominy before the universe' and the 'grubby company of failed African states.'
